t011: Musset is a calm place to write, a manuscript you can see whole, a keyboard that never makes you reach for the mouse — and a publisher inside, who reads, questions and annotates. It never writes a word for you.

t015: As calm as a blank page.
t016: Plain text, one column, nothing blinking. Focus mode, typewriter scrolling, a kiosk mode that turns your Mac into a typewriter — and Ultra Focus when the draft has to come out.
t018: Parts, chapters, scenes and statuses. A plot grid. A Bible for characters, places and documents. Two versions of a chapter, side by side, until you choose.
t023: Writing a book is a long silence. Musset gives you someone to talk to while you write: an editor you can question, push back on, argue with — about your text, as it takes shape. It quotes your sentence, says what it sees, and asks a question. The words stay yours: Musset never writes a line for you.
t024: Creativity needs a channel. Start from what readers of your genre expect, or hand over your own style guide, constraints and goals. The editor holds you to them, chapter after chapter.
t025: ●Genre presets — literary fiction, crime, romance, fantasy, science fiction, YA, historical, horror and more: the expectations a publisher in your genre reads with, every judgment backed by a quotation.
t026: ●Your style guide, your constraints, your goals — write them once; each chapter is read against them, in the margin.
t027: ●Kept on track — continuity, tics, facts to check, and the scene that drifts from what you set out to do.
t028: ●What works, too — a good editor says so. Praise has its own colour.
t029: An AI editor does not, and never will, replace a human one. Its job is to help: to point at the key issues while you write. The finesse and judgment of a real editor remain human — Musset gets your manuscript ready for that conversation, it doesn’t stand in for it.
t030: Uses your own Claude or ChatGPT subscription. Everything works with the AI switched off.
t032: Ask about the chapter you’re in, the way you would ask an editor over coffee: does this scene hold, is the ending too soon, where does the tension drop? The answer comes from your text — and what it points at lands in the margin, as notes you can take or leave.
t033: One click runs a full reading: style, tics, continuity, what to cut, the opening and the ending, facts to check.

t036: In line with the Authors Guild’s Human Authored certification.
t037: The certification asks that every word of the book be written by a person, allowing only spelling and grammar checks. That is exactly how Musset works: the editor reads, questions and annotates; the proofreader fixes typos and agreement, one word at a time. Nothing in Musset generates your prose — and the code is open, so anyone can check.
t039: ✓ Critique in the margin, never rewrites
t040: ✓ Spelling and grammar, word by word
t042: Musset is not affiliated with the Authors Guild. The certification is yours to claim, for books published in the United States (in the UK, through the Society of Authors).
t045: Pick the keys your hands already know, in Settings. ⌘ stays Musset’s in every mode, and AZERTY keyboards are handled.

t054: Modes and motions that understand prose: sentences, paragraphs, scenes.
t057: The mark, the kill ring, Meta by Esc — and ⌥ still types your accents.
t060: No interface, no going back. Choose how strict: Light lets you mend the sentence you’re in, Normal lets you backspace, Hardcore lets you do neither. What you wrote lands at the end of the chapter.
t065: All of Musset is one keystroke away.
t066: ⌘K goes to any chapter or scene, in any of your books, runs a critique, searches the text, switches to dark. No toolbar to learn.
t069: Musset takes the whole screen — menu bar, Dock and notch included. No notifications, no other windows, and no switching to another app: ⌘Tab does nothing until you leave. Only your book, your chapters and the page.
t071: The menu bar, the Dock and the window frame disappear.
t073: App switching is off. The internet is one decision further away.
t075: Chapters, notes, Write, Revise and Read stay at hand.
t077: Read it as a book. Send it as a manuscript.
t078: Reading mode sets your chapters in EB Garamond, page by page, as they will print. When it’s time to submit, Musset lays out the manuscript the way publishers in your country expect it — and counts it the way they count.
t080: Your PDF looks like a book, because it is set like one.
t081: Musset typesets with Typst, a modern engine in the tradition of TeX, in EB Garamond — a revival of the sixteenth-century Garamond type. The pages below come straight out of Musset, untouched.
t083: Each paragraph is set as a whole, not line by line: even spacing between words, hyphenation by the rules of the book’s language.

t099: Entering a prize? Send it under a pseudonym, without your name or address. Working with an editor? Export to Word, get their tracked changes back as corrections — each tagged with who made it.
t103: Typography that knows where you write.
t104: Each book has its language and its variant. Musset sets the quotes, dashes and spaces your publisher expects, as you type, and checks spelling and grammar with LanguageTool — on your Mac, nothing sent anywhere.
t117: The interface speaks all six, too — and Brazilian and European Portuguese each get their own.
t119: No more “chapter-3-final-v2-REAL.docx”. Musset quietly keeps every state of your book as you write: you never save a copy, never rename a file, and nothing you delete is ever really gone.
t121: Hesitating between two directions for a chapter? Write both. Read them next to each other, with what differs marked, and choose which one goes in the book. Change your mind whenever you like.
t123: Want to try something bold on the whole book? Do it in a parallel draft, and the real manuscript doesn’t move. Bring back what works, paragraph by paragraph.
t125: See your book as it was last Tuesday, or the day you sent it to your agent. Mark the moments that matter — a submission, a reading — and return to them in one click.
t126: Behind it all is git — the system the whole software world relies on to keep track of its work. You never have to see it. Your chapters stay plain text files you can open anywhere, and the whole history comes with you if you ever leave.
t128: Your editor’s pen, in your text.
t129: Corrections show where they belong: what goes struck through, what comes in green, comments on the passage they’re about. Accept or refuse each one — or all at once.
t130: Who said what. Every correction carries its author’s name.
t131: Your own edits too. Switch to Revise and your changes become corrections you can weigh later.
t132: Editors who live in Word. Send them a .docx; their tracked changes come back as corrections.
t133: Compare anything. Any two moments of a chapter, what changed, side by side.
t135: Sync between your Macs that actually works.
t136: Write on the laptop on the train, pick up on the desk at home. Musset syncs the book with its whole history — every version, every note — not a copy of a file that might be stale.
t138: Your book lives on your Mac. Write without a connection; it syncs when you’re back.
t140: Versions, parallel drafts and milestones follow you from one Mac to the other.
t142: Invite an editor or beta readers. Their changes come back as corrections you accept or refuse, and you can see who wrote what.

title: Musset — the Mac app for people who finish books
description: Musset is a writing app for the Mac, for people who finish books: a calm editor, a manuscript you can see whole, and Musset Reader for your editor on iPhone and iPad.
open_free: Open source under the GPL v3: anyone can read the code, nothing is hidden
n12: A novel is never one page. It is the chapter you are in, the one it answers, the notes you took in March and the map of a town. Musset opens each of them in a tab and sets them side by side: left, right, above, below.
n14: Chapters, Bible sheets, cork boards, the synopsis, the plot grid, the book’s history. One click to look; start working in it and it stays.
n16: Drag a chapter or a sheet from the sidebar onto the side of a pane and it opens there. Drag a tab to move it. Nothing to set up.
n18: Write a scene and its echo forty pages later, each in its pane, each with its own undo. The same chapter in two panes is one text.
n20: Keep the panes as “Drafting” or “Revision” and call them back from the keyboard. The book reopens the way you left it.
n22: Musset with two panes: a chapter being written on the left, a cork board of the novel on the right.
n32: Every novelist ends up with index cards, a wall and a ball of string. Musset’s cork boards live inside the book: pin a character, a place and its map, a scrap of dialogue, and draw the line between them.
n33: Cards from the Bible — drop a character or a place on the board and its sheet becomes a card.
n34: Arrows that hold — they catch the side of a card and stay with it when you move it.
n35: A pen and a highlighter — circle, underline, cross out. Notes, labels, shapes and columns, one key each.
n36: It follows the text — beside a chapter, the cards of the people and places in the paragraph you are writing light up.
n37: A board is a JSON Canvas file in your book’s folder: an open format, readable without Musset.
n38: A cork board in Musset, in dark mode: character and place cards, notes, columns, arrows and pen strokes.
n42: You should not have to stop writing to update a character sheet. Musset reads the chapters as they come and keeps the cast: who appears, how often, under which names.
n44: A sheet has two parts. Yours: whatever you want to remember. And the book’s: what your chapters actually state about this person, each with the chapter it comes from. When two chapters disagree, you are told.
n46: Claire becomes Hélène in every chapter, note and sheet. You see each line before it changes, the doubtful ones set apart. One change, one undo.
n48: Give a place an address and its map comes with it. Pin photographs, documents and sources to any sheet.
n49: The Bible is a folder of Markdown files inside your book. Musset files what it finds; the folders you made stay as you made them.
n50: A character’s sheet in Musset: what the book says about her, and the author’s own notes.
n51: The cast of a novel in columns: main characters, secondary characters, passers-by.
n62: Pull a tab out of the window and it becomes a window of its own. Keep the chapter on the laptop and park the board and the Bible on the big screen. Close the lid; tomorrow every window is where it was.
n63: A tab dragged out of the window opens in its own.
n64: Each window has its panes and tabs, and all of them come back with the book.
n65: The same chapter in two windows is one text, saved once.
n66: A laptop showing a chapter in Musset’s editor.
n67: A second screen showing a window of Musset with a character sheet and a cork board side by side.
n72: A chapter of several scenes is hard to hold in your head. One key lays its scenes side by side like index cards, each with its whole text: you see the order, change it, and go back to writing.
n74: Not a summary: the scene’s own text, in the editor’s type, with its word count. Make the cards smaller to see the whole chapter, larger to read.
n76: Pick a card up by its header and put it down elsewhere: the text follows. Nothing to cut, nothing to paste.
n78: Point between two paragraphs to split a scene there. Merge it with the next one from its menu. Double-click a title to change it.
n79: From the book down to the scene.
n80: The overview shows every chapter with how it opens and how it closes. Step into a part, where scenes move from one chapter to another, then into a chapter.
n82: A chapter in Musset shown as scenes: three scenes side by side, each with its whole text and its word count.
n83: The book’s overview: its numbers, then each chapter with its opening and its close.
n90: Ultra Focus fills the screen: the chapter so far, dimmed, and under it the sentence being written. Nothing else but the way out, in a corner.

m_title: Musset will never write a word of your book.
m_text: Every writing tool now offers to write for you. Musset refuses. Its AI works the way a publisher’s reader does: it reads the chapter, quotes your sentence, says what it sees and asks a question. What you do next is up to you.
s_title: One app, where there used to be five.

mn1: Mac only. No Windows, no iPad. Musset is made for the desk where a book gets written, and for nothing else.
mn2q: Is my book locked inside Musset?
mn2a: No. It is a folder of plain text files on your Mac. Any editor opens them, with or without Musset.
mn3q: Does my manuscript leave my Mac?
mn3a: Only when you ask for a reading, and then only to the Claude or ChatGPT account you already have. Proofreading runs on your Mac. With the AI off, nothing is sent.
mn4q: Do my readers have to buy anything?
mn4a: No. Musset Reader is free for everyone you invite, and they don’t need a Mac.
mn5: The page you read in Musset is the page the printer gets: same engine, same type, same line breaks.
u_hint: Type a sentence here. Then try to take it back.
pr_sub: Musset is free while it is a beta. From version 1.0 it will cost US$9.90, once, and it stays open source. Sync is the only subscription, and only if you want your books in the cloud.
